requested.title: URL-decoded route param reflected into unsanitized server log line
Upload size limit enforced only after the entire request body is buffered in memory; no rate limit on the route
Unauthenticated form action sleeps 3 s per request with no rate limit — cheap asymmetric resource exhaustion
Unauthenticated POST returns a full server stack trace (deployed site runs in development mode)
Form action name resolved through the prototype chain, bypassing the unknown-action 404 and forcing 500s
Action redirects to a slashless path on a trailingSlash: 'always' site, costing an extra 301 hop

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Verified end-to-end. Bun route params reach the resolver URL-decoded — asserted twice in-repo: the code comment at Mochi.ts:1463 ('Route params are URL-decoded and may contain `../`') and the live test at file.test.ts:118-126, which proves an encoded `../` chain arrives verbatim. The ALLOWED miss calls `error(404, ...)`, which throws `MochiHttpError` (utils/index.ts:82-92) carrying the decoded `name` as `.message`. The file-route catch block takes the `instanceof MochiHttpError` branch at Mochi.ts:1497-1501 and does `logger.error(`${req.method} ${url.pathname} → ${err.status}: ${err.message}`)`; utils/log.ts:38-43 forwards that straight to `console.error` with no escaping or control-character stripping, and the site's `logger: { level: 'log' }` (index.ts:199) is level 4, so `error` (1) is emitted. I found a second sink the finding missed: line 1500's `emitError('file', …)` copies the same message onto the `error` event, which consoleLogger renders into an `ERR` line (dev/consoleLogger.ts:162-167), and the site's `consoleLogger:line` filter only nulls `/health` paths — so one request forges lines through two independent console writers. The finding's own negatives also check out: `url.pathname` stays percent-encoded (URL parsing preserves it), so that half of the line is safe; traversal is genuinely dead (exact-match Set, plus realpath + `path.relative` containment + `isExcludedDotPath` at Mochi.ts:1466-1485); and the body is `text/plain; charset=utf-8`, so no XSS. This is CWE-117, trivially reachable unauthenticated on the deployed site. Keeping MEDIUM only because no lower security tier exists in this scheme — the real-world impact is log forgery on container stdout, the bottom of that band. One honest caveat: per the static-only constraint I did not execute a request, so Bun's specific handling of `%0A` in a `:name` segment is inferred from the repo's own documented decoding behaviour rather than observed; nothing in the path filters control bytes.

The mechanics are right but the finding is misattributed, and its concrete attack is not established. (1) The flagged lines cannot be the defect. Bun buffers the entire request body in its HTTP layer before `await req.formData()` (Mochi.ts:1077) resolves, which is before any handler code runs — so no edit at lines 7/16/19 changes the memory profile at all. `file.size > 100 * 1024` is input validation for what the demo will echo back, and nothing in the code or the rendered page advertises it as a resource control. The finding concedes this itself: its actual recommendation targets `Mochi.serve()` in index.ts, i.e. a different file. (2) The real gap is an absent hardening default, not a flaw here: `maxRequestBodySize` is reachable only through the `bun` escape hatch (types.ts:469, docs/160-serve-options.md:83), the site sets no `bun` option, so Bun's 128 MB default (bun-types/serve.d.ts:841-845) applies identically to every POST route in every Mochi app — `/demos/form-cancel`, `/demos/reload-form-data`, the support form, all of them. Singling out this route adds nothing. (3) The 'deviation from the site's own convention' premise is factually backwards. I surveyed every action-bearing demo: 11 of 13 carry no `rateLimit`; only `queue` and `reload-form-data` do, and their inline comments show why — both write shared state other visitors see (a durable queue, a module-level guestbook array), so the limit is an anti-spam control for persistent content, not a generic DoS baseline. `file-upload` echoes the submitter's own bytes back and stores nothing. (4) The project's own known-FP guidance says to judge `packages/site/src/demos/*` as documentation, not product. (5) Suggestive but unverifiable from the repo: the deployment is CapRover with nginx as the socket peer for every visitor (index.ts:169, :200), and nginx caps request bodies — its stock `client_max_body_size` is 1 MB, which would 413 the ~128 MB bodies the attack needs long before Bun allocated anything. I could not read that value from the repo, so I rest the verdict on (1)-(4). Setting `maxRequestBodySize` on the serve call is still worthwhile hardening — just not a vulnerability in this file.

Every individual fact checks out — `buildLimiter()` (Mochi.ts:806-818) does return null when neither a route-level nor a global `rateLimit` exists and the site sets neither; `KIND_POLICY.page.timeout` is true so `server.timeout(req, 0)` disables Bun's per-request timeout (requestSetup.ts:63, 85-87); the protection gate really is scoped to `/demos/protection*` (index.ts:191); and `csrfCheck` really is not an abuse control, since a non-browser client just sets the Origin header. But the conclusion does not follow, because `Bun.sleep(3000)` does not consume an exhaustible resource. What accumulates per in-flight request is an idle timer, a Request, a parsed FormData and an AsyncLocalStorage frame — single-digit KB and zero CPU. The finding's own figure, ~1500 concurrent pending requests, is routine for an event-loop server; 1500 idle timers is not a DoS. The scarce resources are CPU for the SSR re-render and connection slots, and the sleep amplifies neither — it *throttles* the attacker, since the same connection could drive the identical `renderComponent` 3x faster against any other page POST, or against a plain GET of any page on the site with no delay at all. So this is one of the more expensive levers for an attacker, not the cheapest. The '~128 MiB in query' amplifier is the same site-wide Bun default as F2, not specific to this route, and is bounded in the deployed nginx/CapRover topology. The 'omission looks accidental' argument is also backwards: I checked all 13 action-bearing demos and 11 have no `rateLimit`; the two that do guard shared-state writes (durable queue, module-level guestbook) and say so in comments. And per the project's known-FP guidance, `packages/site/src/demos/*` is judged as documentation — here the 3 s delay is the literal subject of the demo (it exists so a reader can watch a submission be cancelled mid-flight), not an oversight. Capping `query` and wiring the sleep to `request.signal` are reasonable polish; neither closes a vulnerability.

Every technical claim is correct and I confirmed each one, yet the result is intended, documented product behaviour with no confidentiality impact. Confirmed: `renderErrorResponseInner` gates the stack on `development` alone (runtime/errors.ts:93-97); `DefaultError.svelte:27-31` renders it in a `<pre>`; the site sets no `errorPage` and its `handleError` (index.ts:47-58) returns undefined for this path so nothing overrides; `development = options.development ?? SEEDED_IS_DEV` (Mochi.ts:479) with `resolveEnvDev` = `NODE_ENV === 'development'` (utils/env.ts:12-17); `packages/site/package.json:14` is `NODE_ENV=development bun src/index.ts`; the Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT is `bun run dev:${WORKSPACE}`; build.yml pairs `workspace: site` with `dockerfile: Dockerfile`. A plain curl POST is non-enhanced (`isEnhanceRequest` prefers text/html for a wildcard Accept, formsJson.ts:10-19) and csrfCheckDefault returns null on the dev-mode branch (csrf.ts:160-165), so the request is accepted with no Origin. So yes — an unauthenticated POST returns a stack. But: the dev-mode deployment is a deliberate, twice-documented decision, not a misconfiguration — build.yml:36-39 says 'Main demo site. Deployed in dev mode ... so the debug toolbar and dev overlays are visible', and the Dockerfile header repeats it. The error page's stack trace is one of those dev overlays. This demo's entire stated purpose is to render it: FormErrors.svelte labels the second form 'Plain POST, server throws, Mochi renders the error page (press back to return)', with a visible button, so no attack is involved — it is the documented interaction. The disclosed data has no confidentiality value: the frames point into fully public open-source code at `/usr/src/app/...` paths published in the repo's own Dockerfile. The 'confirms the site runs in dev mode' angle adds nothing either, since the debug toolbar already advertises that on every page by design. The log-amplifier sub-claim is equally non-distinguishing — `?/missing` on any action route already renders an error page. The framework-design critique (gate stacks on an explicit opt-in rather than on `development`) is a fair suggestion for `runtime/errors.ts`, but it matches SvelteKit/Next/Remix behaviour and is not a defect in this demo route.

Confirmed in full, including every supporting claim. `MochiFormActions` is `Record<string, MochiFormActionHandler>` (types.ts:153) and this route declares it as an object literal, so the prototype is `Object.prototype`. At Mochi.ts:1050-1058, `actionName` is the first query-string key starting with '/' — fully attacker-controlled — and the lookup is a bare `livePostActions[actionName]` guarded only by `if (!actionHandler)`, which inherited members defeat. Both branches of line 1045 hand over the user's literal unchanged: `pageConfigMap` is dev-only (line 767) and stores the same object reference (line 891), while production captures `actions` directly, so this reproduces in both modes. `?/toString` resolves `Object.prototype.toString`, truthy and callable; `packages/mochi/package.json` is `"type": "module"`, so ESM strict mode makes `this === undefined` and the call returns the string '[object Undefined]'. I verified all three result predicates are marker-based and reject a string (`typeof v === 'object'` short-circuits — forms.ts:37-47), so execution falls to lines 1165-1167 and the page re-renders at HTTP 200 with `ctx.form = { ok: true, action: 'toString', data: {} }` plus an `action:complete` 'success' event — a nonexistent action producing a successful-submission render instead of the intended 404. `?/__proto__` resolves to `Object.prototype`, truthy but not callable, so the invocation at 1102 throws TypeError, is caught at 1115, and maps to 500 via `routeErrorResponse`; that half holds regardless of strict mode. `?/valueOf` and `?/hasOwnProperty` throw the same way under strict mode. No RCE: only one lookup level, and `?/constructor` gives `Object`, which merely returns its argument. The precedent argument is the strongest part and it is accurate: image/config.ts:82-83 uses `Object.create(null)` with a comment naming this exact hazard, `getSize` adds `Object.hasOwn` (:164-166), and config.test.ts:82 already regression-tests `['toString','constructor','hasOwnProperty','__proto__']`; highlight.server.ts:33-41 does the same with `Object.assign(Object.create(null), aliases)` + `Object.hasOwn`. The action dispatch — the only one of the three whose key comes straight off the query string — has neither, and enhance.test.ts:286 covers only `?/missing`. Impact is bounded (no cross-user reach, since production CSRF stops browser-driven cross-site POSTs, so it is self-inflicted state confusion plus unauthenticated 500/error-telemetry generation on every action route of every Mochi app), which keeps it at MEDIUM rather than higher. The fix belongs at Mochi.ts:1057 (`Object.hasOwn` + a `typeof === 'function'` assertion), as the finding recommends.

Verified, and correctly filed as a BUG rather than a security issue. The site sets `trailingSlash: 'always'` (index.ts:172) while line 11 redirects to `/demos/form-redirects?redirected=1` with no trailing slash. Page routes are the only kind that mirror both slash forms (`mirrorsSlashForm` reads `KIND_POLICY[kind].trailingSlash`, true only for `page` — requestSetup.ts:62-78), so the slashless pattern is registered and the request matches rather than 404ing; `buildRequestContext` then runs `trailingSlashRedirect`, and with policy 'always' on a dot-free pathname that is not slash-exempt it returns `permanentRedirect(method, pathname + '/' + url.search)` — a 301 for GET (trailingSlash.ts:19-21, 52-55). So the browser makes three requests where two would do, and because `url.search` is re-attached the query survives: behaviour is correct, the cost is a wasted round trip. The documentation angle also checks out — RedirectDemo.svelte prints `location: "{redirectResult.location}"` verbatim on the enhanced path, so the non-canonical URL is literally what the demo shows the reader. So does the inconsistency claim: image-invalidation/routes.ts:25 redirects to the canonical `/demos/image-invalidation/`, while login/routes.ts:35 repeats the slashless form. Adding the slash in both places is the right fix.
